title: Assessing quality, reliability and accuracy of polycystic ovary syndrome-related content on TikTok: A video-based cross-sectional analysis
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of 120 English-language TikTok videos retrieved with the keyword 'PCOS' (30 April 2024). Beyond the quality instruments (PEMAT A/V, mDISCERN, GQS, VIQI), every video was fact-checked against established PCOS guidelines and the literature and placed in one of three misinformation bands; 56.7% were 'partially accurate' (25-50% false information) and 6.6% 'inaccurate or uninformative' (>50% false information), 'accounting for 63.3% of the evaluated material'. That is a quantitative share of items judged against external ground truth with a stated denominator, so CONTENT. The quality instruments are reported only as medians and generate no rows.

estimates.country: Not reported for the videos (creators' country of origin was recorded but never tabulated); English-language videos only, search run from Italy on a newly created account
estimates.measure_type: % of English-language PCOS videos on TikTok containing at least 25% false information (partially accurate plus inaccurate/uninformative)
estimates.value_raw: '56.7% classified as partially accurate (with 25%-50% of false information) and 6.6% deemed uninformative (more than 50% of false information), accounting for 63.3% of the evaluated material'; Table 2 counts: partially accurate 68 (56.7), inaccurate or uninformative 8 (6.6) of 120
estimates.denominator: 120 TikTok videos deemed suitable for analysis out of 300 reviewed (107 off-topic, 51 non-English, 2 removed from the platform, 20 duplicates excluded); 64 by healthcare professionals, 56 by PCOS patients
estimates.definition: Videos were graded by the proportion of false information they carried: 'inaccurate or misinformative' if more than 50% false information, 'partially accurate' if 25%-50% false information, 'accurate and evidence-based' if <25% misinformation. Misinformation was assessed 'by evaluating inaccurate claims about etiology, promotion of unproven treatments, omission of critical information about risks and complications, erroneous dietary advice or claims about fertility.' This row's numerator is the two non-accurate bands combined.
estimates.misinfo_def: No standalone definition; operationally 'each video underwent a fact-checking process to identify and address any misinformation. This process used established PCOS guidelines and existing literature.'
estimates.source_quote: and 6.6% deemed uninformative (more than 50% of false information), accounting for 63.3% of the evaluated material.
estimates.page_loc: Results, section 3.2 'Misinformation evaluation', p. 278; Table 2 'Misinformation assessment', p. 279
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Evaluation team of one senior gynecologist specialising in PCOS and reproductive endocrinology (GR) and two Obstetrics and Gynecology residents (RMC, CC), all at University of Campania 'Luigi Vanvitelli'. 'To ensure objectivity, each team member independently reviewed and scored the videos. Any discrepancies in the evaluations were resolved by a further review conducted by another gynecologist (AE)' from the University of Palermo, establishing consensus. External benchmark: 'established PCOS guidelines and existing literature' (refs 30-32; the 2023 international evidence-based PCOS guidelines / revised Rotterdam criteria are cited in the Introduction). No kappa or percent-agreement statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: On April 30, 2024, a search was executed on TikTok using the keyword “PCOS.” A new account was created specifically for this study to minimize the impact of personalized content generated by the platform's algorithm. The search results were generated using the platform's default algorithm settings, without any modifications, to ensure an unbiased preliminary selection with retained validity.
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT FOR ADJUDICATOR - denominator error in the source: the ABSTRACT states 'A total of 180 videos were included', but the Results state 'Of the 300 videos reviewed, 120 were deemed suitable for analysis. A total of 180 videos were excluded', and every table totals 120 (44 + 68 + 8 = 120; 64 healthcare professionals + 56 patients = 120; 44/120 = 36.7%, 68/120 = 56.7%, 8/120 = 6.67%). The correct denominator is 120; the abstract's '180 included' is a mis-statement of the number EXCLUDED. SECOND CAVEAT: the bands measure the SHARE OF EACH VIDEO that is false, not whether a video contains any falsehood - the 'accurate and evidence-based' band still permits up to 25% misinformation - so 63.3% is 'videos at least a quarter of whose content is false', and the share of videos containing ANY misinformation is unknown and would be higher. Confidence set to medium for these two reasons. 63.3% is printed verbatim by the authors, so it is not a cross-category sum computed by the extractor. Denom_selection=curated because the sample is whatever TikTok's default algorithm surfaced for one keyword on one day (the authors flag this as a limitation). QUOTE NOTE: the v2txt file interleaves the two PDF columns line by line, so the full sentence is not a contiguous span of the text file; source_quote is the longest contiguous span that carries the value. Full sentence: "A substantial portion of the videos were considered either partially accurate or lacking in informative value, with 56.7% classified as partially accurate (with 25%-50% of false information) and 6.6% deemed uninformative (more than 50% of false information), accounting for 63.3% of the evaluated material."

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The middle band on its own, 'partially accurate' 68/120 (56.7%), was not written as a separate row because it overlaps the 63.3% row (it is one of its two components) and is not a cumulative threshold. Its complement, 'accurate and evidence-based' 44/120 (36.7%), is likewise not extracted. 2) Author-type splits are verbatim in Table 2 but are actor-type subgroups within one platform x country cell, so no rows: accurate and evidence-based 40/64 (62.5%) healthcare professionals vs 4/56 (7.2%) patients; partially accurate 24/64 (37.5%) vs 44/56 (78.4%); inaccurate or uninformative 0/64 (0%) vs 8/56 (14.4%). 3) NO QUALITY rows written: every quality instrument is reported only as a median with IQR and range, never as a share of videos above a threshold - PEMAT A/V understandability 50% (IQR 33-58), actionability 25% (IQR 25-50), mDISCERN 2 (IQR 1-3), VIQI total 12 (IQR 10-15), GQS 3 (IQR 2-4) (Table 3). The paper defines thresholds (mDISCERN >=3 = high reliability; GQS >=3 = high quality) but never reports what proportion of videos met them. 4) Other Table 2 content flags are not veracity judgements and get no rows: describes alternatives to hormone therapy 34/120 (28.7%); encourages avoiding hormone therapy 0/120 (0%); encourages distrust of gynecologist 4/120 (3.3%); increases anxiety/concern 32/120 (26.7%); tone negative 30/120 (25%). 5) '45% of TikTok content' with conflicts of interest is cited from Naroji et al. (ref 34), not this paper's data - excluded under R8. 6) Engagement metrics (Table 1: median 42,100 views, 3,233 likes, 11,800 shares) are never expressed as a share going to misinformative videos, so no EXPOSURE or SHARING row. 7) SECOND TABLE ERROR for the record: Table 2 'Purpose - Storytelling' prints healthcare professionals as '2 (31.2)' where 2/64 = 3.1%; the counts (2 + 30 = 32) are consistent, the percentage is a typo. Also 8/56 = 14.3%, printed as 14.4%.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content and quality analysis of an algorithm-surfaced TikTok set. Frame: one keyword search ('PCOS') executed on 30 April 2024 from a newly created account (to blunt personalisation), default algorithm sort; 300 videos reviewed, 120 included after excluding 107 off-topic, 51 non-English, 2 platform-removed and 20 duplicates. Not a probability sample; the authors concede 'The video selection process, influenced by TikTok's algorithm and its sensitivity to specific keywords, may have introduced bias, potentially impacting the generalizability of our results.' No response rate applies. Coding: three team members (one senior gynecologist specialising in PCOS, two OB/GYN residents) independently reviewed and scored every video on PEMAT A/V, mDISCERN, GQS, VIQI and a three-band misinformation classification; discrepancies were resolved by a further review from an independent gynecologist at another university, producing consensus. No inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa, ICC or percent agreement) is reported anywhere. Statistics: Shapiro-Wilk, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's test, Spearman correlations, STATA 14.1. IRB approval not required (public data). Key internal inconsistency: the abstract's 'A total of 180 videos were included' contradicts the Results and all tables, which analyse 120.
